title: Spring Security basics

richText: Authentication and authorization
Spring Security controls access to a Spring web application.
Authentication checks who the user is. A password login is one way to authenticate.
Authorization checks what that user is allowed to do.
These examples use Spring Boot 3 and Spring Security 6. Boot 3 requires Java 17 or later.
Add Spring Security
Add spring-boot-starter-security to the project.
For a servlet web application, Boot protects requests and supplies a default login page when you have not supplied your own security configuration.
Boot creates a user named user with a generated password when no custom authentication setup replaces it. The startup log contains that password.
Define a SecurityFilterChain bean to choose request rules and the login method.
Boot configures web security when the starter is present. You do not need @EnableWebSecurity solely to activate it in a Boot application.
WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter and antMatchers belong to older Spring Security code. Use SecurityFilterChain and requestMatchers in these notes.
Define users and passwords
UserDetailsService loads the user account needed for password authentication.
InMemoryUserDetailsManager keeps user accounts in application memory. Restarting the application does not preserve changes to these accounts.
PasswordEncoder hashes a password and checks a submitted password against the stored hash. Hashing is not reversible encryption.
Hash the password when creating or changing it. During login, use matches to compare the submitted password with its stored hash.
Use in-memory users for learning or isolated checks. Use persistent account storage when users must survive restarts.

roles("USER") stores the authority ROLE_USER. The role is used in the next lesson.

formLogin supplies Spring’s login page. After successful login, Spring remembers authentication in the browser session.
